questions.explanation: A climate classification is a scheme for sorting places by their long-term atmospheric conditions, and for that to work at all the sorting has to be reproducible by someone who has never been to the place. That requires thresholds stated in advance and expressed in measurable quantities, which in practice means averages of temperature and precipitation taken over a standard period, usually thirty years, together with a stated rule for which station or grid cell represents the location. The reason thirty years keeps appearing is that a shorter period makes the classes unstable: a single cold decade would move many stations across a boundary, and the map of world climates would change for reasons that are climatological noise. The fourth option is not as wrong as it looks, since vegetation does integrate climate closely and the boundaries of the biome map resemble those of the climate map, but using the consequence to define the cause is circular. The second and third are simply not classification at all: one is administrative, the other a value judgement, and neither can be checked against a measurement.

questions.explanation: The letter encodes the group, and the letter is chosen so that the alphabetical order of the groups roughly follows warmth. questions.explanation: The shadow is made by two temperature changes in sequence, and both matter. Air forced up a slope expands as the pressure falls, and expanding air cools, so water vapour condenses into cloud and falls as rain on the windward side. By the time the air reaches the crest it has given up a large share of its moisture. It then descends the leeward slope, compressing and warming at roughly the dry adiabatic rate, which is faster than the rate it cooled on the way up, so it arrives at the low ground warmer and drier than the air that left the other side of the mountain. The descending air therefore holds a relative capacity to take up water, which is what suppresses rainfall behind the range and can even suppress it further downwind as the air continues to dry. The second option has the sign of the temperature change wrong, and the third and fourth each miss the mechanism in favour of a simpler story that does not survive a case where the range is small but the wind is strong.

questions.explanation: A monsoon is defined by a seasonal reversal of the prevailing wind, and the reversal is a temperature effect. Land warms and cools faster than water, so in the warm season the land surface is hotter, the air above it rises, and the pressure falls, drawing wind from the sea onshore. In the cool season the pattern inverts: the land is cooler, the pressure over it is relatively higher, and the wind blows offshore. The direction of the wind therefore flips twice a year, and because it carries moisture in one direction and is dry in the other, the rainfall regime is seasonal and often sharply so, with the bulk of the year's rain arriving during the onshore phase. This is why a monsoon is not simply a very wet climate, and why two places on the same latitude with the same annual rainfall can have completely different rainfall seasons. The second option describes the absence of seasonality, the third the absence of a reversal, and the fourth an ocean current, which does affect rainfall but is not what the word means.

questions.explanation: A teleconnection is a mechanism by which an anomaly in one part of the circulation alters conditions in another, far away, through the way the atmosphere and oceans are coupled. In an El Nino event, weakened trade winds allow warm water to shift eastwards across the Pacific, which warms the eastern equatorial sea surface. That warms the air above it, and the rising air changes the pattern of upper-level outflow, so the descending branch of the Walker circulation weakens and the rising branch over Indonesia is suppressed. The consequence reaches far beyond the Pacific because the cells that drive the global circulation are linked, and the changed position of one of them shifts the jet streams and the position of the Hadley cell over other continents. That is why an event in the equatorial Pacific is associated with wetter or drier seasons in places as far apart as Australia and the Gulf of Mexico. The second and third options each deny the distance, and the fourth is the important distinction: a teleconnection is a physical mechanism, and the evidence for it is that the link persists across many events and survives attempts to find other explanations.

A regional temperature trend is the change in the mean over a large area and a long period, and it is a background signal that a city sits inside: if the countryside warms by a degree over forty years, the city most probably warms as well, and that shared change is not a heat island. answer.exemplar: A drought is not a single condition but a departure from the rainfall a place normally receives, accumulated over a period long enough to matter, and the declaration is an act of government that turns that departure into an administrative status with consequences attached. Because rainfall varies enormously from place to place, there is no figure of rainfall that is drought anywhere in general, so the declaration has to be expressed relative to a baseline for the location concerned, and the accumulated deficit is the usual measure: rainfall received over weeks or months set against the long-term average for the same calendar period, which captures the fact that a mild wet winter followed by a dry spring can produce a genuine agricultural emergency. Two further conditions are normally folded in, because a rainfall deficit does not by itself say what is failing: a measure of soil moisture or reservoir storage, and a measure of the effect, such as crop condition or the number of households on emergency supply. The threshold is the part that has to be published, and the reason is that a declaration is a decision about what happens next. It triggers restrictions on abstraction, opens relief schemes, and changes what insurers and aid agencies will pay. A declaration with no stated indicator and no stated number can be disputed by anyone whose interest depends on the outcome, and can be varied after the event to suit a later judgement. Naming the indicator and the number also makes the declaration auditable, so that a later government can be asked whether the condition it declared had actually been met.

questions.explanation: The answer has to make three points, and the third is the one most often dropped. First, that the underlying condition is a deficit accumulated over a stated period rather than a shortage on a particular day. Second, that the deficit is relative to a location-specific baseline, because what counts as dry is not the same everywhere and a single national figure would be meaningless. Third, that a declaration is an administrative act with consequences, so it has to publish its indicator and its number, both so that it can be checked later and so that those affected can act on it. A response that treats drought as purely a hydrological fact misses the third point entirely, and a response that lists the consequences without explaining the relative baseline has not said how the condition is identified. The closing point is worth making explicitly, that the indicator and the threshold are what make the declaration a measurement rather than an opinion, and that a declaration based on an unstated criterion cannot be audited after the event.
questions.hint: Cover the accumulated deficit, the local baseline, and why the declared number matters.

answer.exemplar: The standard form expresses risk as the product of hazard, exposure and vulnerability. The hazard term is the physical event or condition, described by its frequency and its intensity, so it is a property of the physical world and it does not change because of anything anyone does. The exposure term is the presence of people, property and activity in the path of that hazard, and it is a property of the settlement pattern, so it is the term that most often changes over a planning period: a flood of the same magnitude floods a great deal more of a city that has grown into the flood plain. The vulnerability term describes how badly the exposed things are affected, and it depends on construction, preparedness and social capacity, so it is the term that policy can most directly move. Their product matters because the three are not additive. A severe hazard in a place with nothing exposed produces no loss, and a mild hazard in a place with a great deal exposed and poor construction can produce a catastrophe, which is why a ranking of places by hazard alone is not a ranking by risk. The equation is also an accounting identity rather than a physical law, and its practical value is that it tells an analyst where the leverage is: mitigation work normally attacks vulnerability, planning policy attacks exposure through land-use control, and nothing in the arithmetic can reduce the hazard itself.

questions.explanation: The answer earns its keep by saying what each term is a property of and, above all, by explaining why the three are multiplied rather than added. A response that lists the three terms and stops is the common failure, and it leaves the most important consequence unstated, namely that a place can be low-risk because nothing is exposed even though the hazard is severe, and equally can be high-risk on a mild hazard. The second point to make is that the terms are not equally responsive to intervention: the hazard is fixed, exposure changes only slowly and mainly through planning, and vulnerability is the term that preparedness and construction standards act on directly. A third point worth including is that the equation is a way of organising the argument rather than a measurement in itself, since all three terms have to be estimated and each estimate carries its own uncertainty. The closing observation, that the equation is what tells an analyst which of the three levers to pull, is what distinguishes a full answer from a list.

answer.exemplar: The hazard is the physical event or condition that can cause harm, described by how often it occurs and how severe it is when it does. It is a property of the physical world: a given flood depth at a given place has a given probability, and nothing anyone decides about housing or roads alters that probability. Exposure is the presence of people, property and activity in the path of the hazard, and it is a property of the settlement pattern, so it is the term that changes most visibly over a planning period. A city that has grown into the flood plain has increased its exposure without the hazard changing at all, which is why exposure is the term land-use control, zoning restrictions, setbacks and buyouts are designed to move. Vulnerability is how badly the exposed things are affected once the hazard arrives, and it depends on construction standards, the age and condition of the building stock, preparedness, and the social capacity of households to respond, so it is the term that building codes, retrofit, warning systems and assistance schemes act on. The division is not a matter of taste. Hazards are effectively fixed over the time scale at which any policy operates, and a policy that claims to reduce the hazard is either describing a very long horizon or misdescribing what it does. Exposure moves slowly and mostly through regulation of what may be built where. Vulnerability moves fastest and is where most of the measurable gains in loss reduction have come from.

questions.explanation: The answer is graded on two things: whether each term is defined as a property of something different, and whether the policy consequences follow from those definitions rather than being asserted alongside them. The critical move is to say that the hazard term is not available to policy, because that is what makes the other two the whole of the practical field, and a response that treats the three as equally manipulable has missed the point. The second requirement is to attach a timescale to each, since exposure moves on a planning cycle and vulnerability moves on a retrofit cycle, and that difference is what explains why a retrofit programme can show measurable savings within a few years while a land-use change takes a generation. The third is to name concrete instruments for the two movable terms, and to note that the instruments are not equivalent: land-use control reduces exposure for new development while doing nothing for the stock already there, so retrofit is what reaches the existing stock. A response that omits the existing stock will be marked down, because that is where most of the loss actually sits.

The second step is to divide that by the area the plan allows per person, here 2.5 square metres, which gives 240 people. The third is to compare the result with the people who are expected, because a capacity figure is only meaningful against a demand figure, and the shortfall between the two is what an evacuation plan has to solve by opening a second site. What the resulting figure leaves out is what cannot be reduced to floor area. The 240 counts bodies, not the conditions they need: the toilets the plan requires to serve them, the drinking water, the cooking and the supplies, the space the ambulances need to reach the entrance, and the hours the building can realistically be occupied before people have to be moved on. questions.explanation: Two distinct effects of wind explain the difference, and they operate on different parts of the fire's behaviour. The first is on the rate of spread: wind supplies oxygen to the advancing flame front and tilts the flame towards unburnt fuel, so a head fire advances at a rate set by the wind speed rather than by the rate at which the fuel burns. The second is on the mechanism of spread: gusts lift embers and burning fragments off the flame front and carry them ahead of it, and where one of those lands on receptive fuel it starts a new fire well beyond the main front, which is how a single fire becomes a landscape fire. questions.explanation: The order runs from the ground up, then forward in time, then to the decision, and only then to the action, because each stage constrains the next. questions.explanation: A slab avalanche requires two things in the pack, and they are a hard cohesive slab and a weak layer beneath it. The slab forms when wind deposits snow onto a surface, and the deposition is firm enough to stand as a roof. The weak layer forms separately, commonly as a persistent weak layer of faceted crystals or a melt-freeze crust from an earlier mild spell, and it survives buried because it is a poor conductor of heat and the insulating snow above it keeps its temperature low. The failure then starts at a point, usually a cornice edge, a rock band or a convex roll in the slope, and it propagates along the weak layer because the layer is continuous and uniformly weak, which is why the whole slab releases rather than a patch of it. The second option has the relationship backwards, since a uniformly bonded pack fails everywhere at once only if it fails at all, and uniform bonding does not produce a propagating fracture. The third confuses the trigger with the surface, and the fourth describes a different failure altogether.

answer.exemplar: Desertification is the process by which land in a dry or seasonally dry region degrades towards the condition of a desert, and it is worth being precise about two things. It is usually measured as a fall in productivity or a fall in the proportion of vegetated ground over a period of years, so it is a trend and not a single bad season, and the land itself may become harder to vegetate even after the pressure is relieved, because the soil structure and the organic matter that holds it together have been lost. The overgrazing mechanism has three stages. Grazing animals remove the plant cover that was intercepting raindrop energy and holding the soil together, so the exposed surface is hit directly by raindrops that break aggregates and carry fine particles away. Those fine particles are then not merely lost but rearranged: they lodge in the pores of the surface layer, and the surface forms a crust that reduces infiltration, so less of the next rain enters the soil and more runs off. The third stage is that the reduced infiltration leaves the plants progressively short of water, so cover thins further and the crust breaks into bare, wind-prone patches. A cover crop interrupts this at the first stage, and it interrupts the others by consequence. A living root mat and its residues absorb the energy of falling rain, bind the surface particles into aggregates that resist both detachment and crusting, and raise the roughness that slows overland flow so that water has longer to infiltrate. It is a measure of the same kind as a contour bund or a terrace, and it is the most direct one available where the problem is the loss of cover itself rather than the volume of water arriving.

questions.explanation: The answer is credited for setting out desertification as a process with stages rather than as a condition, because the stages are what make the causal chain defensible and what a cover crop is then able to interrupt. The three-stage account has to be explicit: removal of cover, then crusting and reduced infiltration as the loosened particles are rearranged, then further thinning of the vegetation as water becomes short. A response that stops at the first stage describes a mechanism and not a process, and misses why the degradation tends to continue after the grazing pressure eases. The second requirement is that the cover crop's effect be traced through those same stages rather than asserted, so the reader can see that intercepting rainfall energy protects the aggregate structure and that protecting infiltration is what keeps water available to plants. The distinction worth drawing at the end is between the two directions a degraded dryland can take, since the same loss of cover exposes the surface to wind as well as water, and a measure that only addresses the water term leaves the wind term running.
questions.hint: Set out the stages from lost cover to crusting to thinning, then show where the crop intervenes.
questions.learningObjective: explain the desertification process and what a cover crop does about it

questions.explanation: A return period is a statement about the whole of the period it names, and it is estimated from a record that has to be long enough to contain events at roughly that rarity. questions.explanation: Maladaptation is the case where a measure reduces risk in the short term and increases exposure or loss in the long term, usually by encouraging further development in the place that has been made to feel safe. A sea wall is a genuine adaptation when it works and is maintained, because it lowers the annual expected loss for the people behind it. The problem is the response it provokes. The value of the land behind the wall rises, because the risk of flooding there is perceived to have fallen, and that higher value is capitalised into more and denser buildings, so the quantity of the thing that a failure would destroy goes up. If the wall is overtopped in a larger event than it was designed for, or is not maintained, the loss is far larger than it would have been in the absence of the wall, and the displacement of poorer households that the rising land values produce is a second, distributional cost. The test for maladaptation is therefore not whether a measure works now but whether it locks in a future that is worse under the conditions in which it fails.

answer.exemplar: A claim that land is a net sink of carbon is a claim about a flux and a stock, and the two need separating. Photosynthesis in vegetation and in soils moves carbon from the atmosphere into living tissue and into organic matter in the ground, and respiration, decay and fire return part of it. A net sink means the second flow is smaller than the first over the period measured, so carbon accumulates in the landscape, and a claim of this kind has to name the period, the boundary of the system and the method used to estimate both flows, since the net is a small difference between two large numbers and is correspondingly sensitive to the method. Most of the accumulation is in soil and in tree biomass rather than in the atmosphere, and that is what makes permanence the decisive assumption. A sink is permanent only if the carbon already taken up stays out of the atmosphere, and the sources of reversal are well established: wildfire and clearance release the biomass directly, drought and harvest reduce the uptake that was going to offset those releases, and a logged forest that is not replanted converts a sink into a source. A future release also does not cancel out evenly against the earlier uptake, because the carbon released enters the atmosphere immediately and its effect on temperature persists, whereas the removals that offset it in an accounting balance were spread over the earlier years. This is why a land-sink claim is assessed by asking what happens in the worst plausible case, and why projects that are credited for the removals they expect are discounted when the expectation is not backed by a commitment to keep the carbon where it is. The permanence assumption is where a land claim becomes a financial claim, and the two should be examined together.

questions.explanation: The answer has to make three distinctions. First, that a net sink is a difference between two fluxes rather than a quantity in itself, which is why the period, the system boundary and the method have to be named and why a small net is a fragile figure. Second, that the carbon accumulates in living biomass and in soil, which is what makes the permanence question the decisive one rather than a detail. Third, and this is the point that distinguishes a full answer, that a later release does not cancel the earlier uptake symmetrically in time, because the release is immediate and persistent while the removals that offset it in an accounting balance were spread across earlier years, so treating a reversal as a mere subtraction understates it. The concluding move is to tie the permanence assumption to the financial claim, since projects that sell or are credited with expected removals are really selling a promise about the future, and a promise that depends on other people's future decisions is worth less than a promise about the present.
questions.hint: Separate flux from stock, then explain why a later release does not cancel the earlier uptake cleanly.
